modeDesc.nouns: Pick the right article, or pick the noun that matches an English meaning. Watch for el día, la mano, el problema and el agua.

tableNotes.articles: Definite (the) and indefinite (a / an, some). The article agrees with the noun in gender and number. Feminine nouns starting with a stressed a- take el / un in the singular (el agua) but stay feminine.
tableNotes.prepositions: Simple prepositions, the only two contractions (a + el = al, de + el = del) and common prepositional phrases.
tableNotes.numbers: 1–100. Up to 29 a number is one word (veintitrés); from 31 it is three (treinta y uno).
tableNotes.readings: Real {lang} text, sentence by sentence, used by the Reading tab.

rules.el: Masculine singular nouns take el, whatever their ending: el libro, el día, el problema.
rules.el|f: Feminine nouns starting with a stressed a- take el in the singular so the two a sounds don’t merge. They stay feminine: el agua fría, las aguas.
rules.la: Feminine singular nouns take la: la casa, la mano, la ciudad.
rules.un|f: Feminine nouns starting with a stressed a- take un in the singular: un agua.

numberNotes.text: Uno shortens to un before a masculine noun (un libro) and becomes una before a feminine one.
Eleven to fifteen have their own words: once, doce, trece, catorce, quince.
Sixteen to nineteen are dieci- plus the digit, as one word: dieciséis, diecisiete, dieciocho, diecinueve.
Twenty-one to twenty-nine are one word, veinti- plus the digit. Veintidós, veintitrés and veintiséis carry an accent.
From thirty the tens end in -enta: treinta, cuarenta, cincuenta, sesenta, setenta, ochenta, noventa.
From thirty-one on, write three words: the ten, y, and the unit (treinta y dos).
A hundred on its own is cien.

personOptions.label: he / she / you formal (él / ella / usted)
they / you all formal (ellos / ellas / ustedes)

tenseOptions.label: Present
tenseOptions.title: Present (presente)
tenseOptions.description: Current or habitual actions: hablo = I speak / I am speaking. Also near-future plans: mañana trabajo.

tenseOptions.label: Preterite
tenseOptions.title: Pretérito indefinido (simple past)
tenseOptions.description: Completed actions at a definite time: ayer hablé = yesterday I spoke.

tenseOptions.label: Imperfect
tenseOptions.title: Pretérito imperfecto (imperfect)
tenseOptions.description: Ongoing or habitual past actions and descriptions: hablaba = I was speaking / I used to speak.

tenseOptions.label: Future
tenseOptions.title: Futuro simple (future)
tenseOptions.description: Future actions: hablaré = I will speak. Endings go on the whole infinitive.

tenseOptions.label: Conditional
tenseOptions.title: Condicional simple (conditional)
tenseOptions.description: Polite requests and hypotheticals: me gustaría = I would like; podría = I could.

functions.label: Ability / permission
functions.description: Can, cannot, may: poder (puedo, puedes), and saber for a learned skill (sé nadar).

functions.label: Necessity / need
functions.description: Have to and need to: tener que + infinitive (tengo que trabajar), necesitar, and impersonal hay que.

functions.label: Desire / wish
functions.description: Want and would like: querer (quiero), the conditional me gustaría.

functions.label: Used to / was
functions.description: Ongoing or habitual past in the imperfect: era, tenía, vivía, iba.

functions.label: Future plans
functions.description: Plans: ir a + infinitive (voy a estudiar), the future (viajaré), or the present with a time word.

functions.label: Likes / preferences
functions.description: Likes: me gusta / me gustan (literally “it pleases me”), me encanta, preferir.

sentenceTypes.label: Negative
sentenceTypes.description: A sentence with no or nunca.

sentenceTypes.label: Request / command
sentenceTypes.description: Asks or tells someone to do something, or orders (Para mí…, Gire a la derecha).

lessons.title: ¡Hola!
lessons.subtitle: Greetings and goodbyes
goals: Greet anyone, at any time of day

steps.text: Spanish greetings depend on the time of day and on how well you know someone. Start with the one that works everywhere.

steps.note: Works with anyone, at any hour. People often add a second greeting: *Hola, buenos días.*
Until lunch, which in Spain is around 2 pm. It’s plural: literally “good days”.
From lunch until it gets dark, around 8 or 9 pm in Spain.
After dark, both to say hello and to say goodbye.

steps.label: Culture
steps.text: Spanish days run late. *Buenas tardes* lasts until dinner, so it’s still the right greeting at 7 pm.

steps.prompt: It’s 10 am and you walk into a bakery. What do you say?
steps.why: It’s morning, so *buenos días*. You can put *hola* in front: *Hola, buenos días.*

steps.prompt: It’s 6 pm and you meet a neighbour on the stairs. What fits best?
steps.why: Afternoon and early evening are *tardes* until it gets dark.

steps.label: Two words for “you”
steps.text: *Tú* is casual: friends, family, children, people your age. *Usted* is polite: strangers, older people, formal settings. In Spain *tú* is used widely, even in shops and cafés; in much of Latin America *usted* is more common.

steps.note: Friendly and safe with almost anyone.

steps.prompt: You meet your friend’s grandmother for the first time. Which question fits?
steps.why: An older person you’ve just met: polite *usted*. *¿Qué tal?* would sound a bit too casual.

steps.note: The standard goodbye, but many people say *hasta luego* even when they won’t see you again soon.

steps.prompt: You’re leaving work and will see your colleagues tomorrow. What do you say?
steps.why: *Hasta mañana* means “until tomorrow”. The other two are greetings.

steps.text: Lucía stops at a café near her office in Madrid. Two words you’ll need: *por favor* (please) and *gracias* (thanks). A *café con leche* is a white coffee, and *aquí tienes* means “here you are”.

lines.it: Buenos días. Un café con leche, por favor.
lines.en: Good morning. A white coffee, please.
wrong: Buenas noches. Un café con leche, por favor.
Adiós. Un café con leche, por favor.

lines.narration: Lucía drinks her coffee and pays.

lessons.title: Me llamo…
lessons.subtitle: Introducing yourself
goals: Say your name and ask someone else’s
Answer when you meet someone new

steps.note: Literally “I call myself”. Treat it as one phrase for now; the grammar comes later.

steps.en: My name is Carlos. And you?

steps.note: Anyone can say it, in any setting.
It describes the speaker: a man says *encantado*, a woman says *encantada*.

steps.prompt: Ana meets someone new. Which is right for her to say?
steps.why: *Encantado / encantada* describes the speaker, and Ana is a woman.

steps.prompt: How do you ask a child their name?

steps.note: *Soy* comes from *ser*, the “to be” for identity and origin. *De* means “from”.

steps.label: Watch out
steps.text: Nationalities take a small letter in Spanish: *soy inglés*, never *soy Inglés*. Like most adjectives, they change for a woman: *inglés* → *inglesa*.

steps.prompt: Emma is from London. What does she say?
steps.why: Emma is a woman, so *inglesa*, with a small *i*.

steps.text: At a language exchange in Seville, Emma meets Javier. *¿Y tú?* means “and you?”, and *Londres* is London.

lines.it: Hola, me llamo Javier. ¿Cómo te llamas?
lines.en: Hi, my name is Javier. What’s your name?
My name is Emma. Nice to meet you.
Pleased to meet you. Where are you from?
I’m English, from London. And you?

lessons.title: ¿Cómo estás?
lessons.subtitle: How are you? Estar
goals: Ask how someone is, casually and politely
Answer on a scale from great to awful

steps.note: Very common, and fine with almost anyone.

steps.prompt: A friend asks *¿Qué tal?* and you’ve had a terrible day. Which answer fits?
steps.why: *Fatal* is the bottom of the scale. Spanish speakers use it often, and cheerfully.

steps.text: Spanish has two verbs for “to be”. *Ser* (*soy de Madrid*, lesson 2) is for who and what you are. *Estar* is for how and where you are right now.

steps.note: Agrees with the speaker: *estoy cansado* (man), *estoy cansada* (woman).

steps.why: How you feel right now takes *estar*. *Soy cansado* would mean you’re a tiring person.

steps.prompt: Laura is happy today. What does she say?

steps.text: Two flatmates meet in the kitchen in the morning. *¿Un café?* means “a coffee?”.

lines.en: Good morning, Marta! How’s it going?
So-so. I’m very tired. And you?

steps.text: Later, Marta goes to the bakery and greets an older neighbour, so she uses *usted*.

lines.it: Buenos días, señora García. ¿Cómo está usted?
lines.en: Good morning, Mrs García. How are you?
wrong: Buenas noches, señora García. ¿Cómo está usted?

lines.en: Very well, thanks. And you, Marta?
